blocks.text: The camera feed wasn't coming from the industrial facility. It was a wireless relay. The real location was somewhere else.

The missing woman was Natalie Price, thirty-one, a bookkeeper for a chain of check-cashing stores. Investigators learned her bosses had been laundering money for a drug trafficking group. Natalie found out, secretly moved $1.2 million of the laundered money into a frozen account, and sent copies of the records to the FBI. Before agents could meet with her, two men took her from her apartment parking lot.
The men wanted to know where the money was. Natalie refused to tell them, knowing that the moment she did, she'd be of no use to them.
The red dust on the floor mats came from a specific type of soil found near old copper mines east of Phoenix.

The yellow rope was marine rope sold at only two stores in the area. One store's cameras showed the same man buying it two days earlier. His phone records placed him near an abandoned mining office in the desert.
At 10:40 p.m., a SWAT team surrounded the building. Natalie was inside, tied to a chair, exhausted and terrified, but alive. Two men were arrested. A third was arrested the next morning at a hotel.
The money stayed frozen. It became evidence in a federal case that put eleven people in prison, including Natalie's former bosses.

Natalie entered witness protection after the trial. Before she left, she sent me a letter through the FBI. She wrote, "You cleaned a car. You could have thrown that photo in the trash. You didn't. I'll never forget that."
I keep a copy of her letter in my locker at work. I still clean cars. I look under every seat.
